title: The Bronze Serpent and the First Victories
summary: Israel defeats the king of Arad at Hormah, then, while traveling around Edom, grows impatient and complains against God and Moses. God sends venomous snakes, and when the people confess their sin, he tells Moses to make a bronze serpent on a pole so that anyone bitten who looks at it will live. Israel then moves north through the lands east of the Dead Sea, finds water at Beer, and defeats Sihon king of the Amorites and Og king of Bashan, taking their land.
story: Chapter 20 closed the old era with the deaths of Miriam and Aaron. Chapter 21 opens the new one, and for the first time since the victory over Amalek at Rephidim (Exodus 17:8-13) Israel wins battles. The victory at Hormah reverses the humiliating defeat at the same place a generation earlier, when the people tried to enter Canaan against God's command (Numbers 14:45). Yet the old pattern of complaint has not disappeared, and the snakes show that the new generation still needs to learn trust. The chapter then carries Israel from the southern wilderness to the plains opposite Jericho, and the defeats of Sihon and Og give Israel its first territory. These victories were remembered for centuries in Israel's worship, and they set the stage for the Balaam story that follows, since Moab has now seen what happened to its neighbors.
historical:
The chapter moves through real regions of the southern Levant: the Negev, the southern desert of Canaan; the Arnon, a deep gorge that runs into the Dead Sea from the east and served as Moab's northern border; the Zered, further south; and the Jabbok, a river flowing into the Jordan from the east. Heshbon, Dibon, and Medeba are towns on the plateau north of the Arnon. Several of these names appear on the Mesha Stele (also called the Moabite Stone), an inscription found in 1868 at Dhiban, ancient Dibon, in which Mesha king of Moab, in the ninth century BC, credits his god Chemosh with victories over Israel. Chemosh appears in verse 29 as the god of Moab.

Some sites in the chapter raise historical questions. Excavations at Tel Arad and at sites proposed for Heshbon have found little or no occupation from the period many date the exodus, and scholars respond in different ways: some argue the ancient names were attached to different sites at the time, some prefer a different date for the events, and some doubt the historical reliability of the itinerary. Verse 14 quotes the Book of the Wars of the LORD, a source now lost, and the chapter also cites a well song and a taunt song about Heshbon, showing that the writer drew on older poetry.
cultural:
Snakes were a real and deadly danger in the deserts of the region, and they carried symbolic weight across the ancient world. In Egypt the cobra was an emblem of royal and divine power, and serpent images were used as protective charms. A small copper snake figure was found by excavators at a shrine in the Timna valley in the southern Arabah, showing that serpent images were known in this region. The word translated fiery serpent in verse 8 (saraph) likely refers to the burning pain of the venom, and the same word is used for the winged figures around God's throne in Isaiah 6.

The practice described in verses 2 and 3, devoting a city to destruction (the Hebrew verb charam, from which comes the noun herem), meant giving it wholly to God, so that its people were killed and its goods destroyed or given to the sanctuary rather than taken as plunder. The Mesha Stele describes Moab doing something similar to an Israelite town in honor of Chemosh, so the practice was known beyond Israel. The poems in verses 27 to 30 are a taunt song: they recall how Sihon had once taken Moabite land and then celebrate Israel's taking it from him in turn.
literary: This chapter is a collection of short episodes linked by travel notes: a battle (verses 1 to 3), the serpent story (4 to 9), an itinerary with poetic fragments (10 to 20), and two campaigns (21 to 35). The serpent story follows a pattern familiar from earlier complaint stories: complaint, judgment, confession, intercession, and deliverance. This time, unlike most earlier complaints, the people admit “We have sinned”. The remedy is surprising: healing comes by looking at an image of the very thing that bit them. The travel section has the feel of a record, with place names in sequence, but it is punctuated by song, and the chapter's last lines echo formal battle reports.

outline.t: Venomous snakes and the bronze serpent
Traveling to Moab, with songs of the road and the well
The defeat of Sihon king of the Amorites
The defeat of Og king of Bashan

doctrines.note: God does not remove the snakes at once but provides a way to live: whoever looks at the bronze serpent survives. Salvation comes by trusting God's provision, not by the people's own remedies.

Looking at the serpent was an act of trust in God's word, not a magic cure. The later destruction of the serpent when Israel began to worship it (2 Kings 18:4) shows that the object had no power apart from God's promise.
The people ask Moses to intercede, and he does, even though they had just spoken against him. Intercession runs throughout Numbers, and here it leads to healing.

words.note: Nachash, serpent or snake, the same word used for the serpent in Genesis 3. The echo may be deliberate: the creature associated with the first rebellion becomes, in bronze, the means of healing. The text does not make the connection explicit, so it is best noted rather than pressed.
Saraph, a fiery serpent. The word likely comes from the root for burning and may describe the effect of the venom. In Isaiah 6 the same word names the seraphim, the fiery beings around God's throne.

Nechoshet, bronze or copper. There is a wordplay in Hebrew between nachash (serpent) and nechoshet (bronze). 2 Kings 18:4 records that the object was later called Nehushtan and had become an object of worship, so Hezekiah broke it up.

Charam, to devote to destruction. It means to give something wholly to God, removing it from ordinary use. In war this involved killing the inhabitants and destroying or dedicating their property. The name Hormah comes from the same root.

christ: Jesus himself draws on this chapter. In John 3:14-15 he says that just as Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in him may have eternal life. The comparison has several points: a people dying under judgment, a remedy provided by God rather than invented by them, a figure lifted up on a pole, and life for anyone who simply looks in trust. In John's Gospel, being lifted up refers to Jesus's crucifixion (John 12:32-33). The bronze serpent was a likeness of what was killing the people; Paul similarly says that God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh to deal with sin (Romans 8:3). The link here is not a Christian invention but Jesus's own reading of the story.

hard.q: How should readers understand Israel's vow to devote Arad's cities to destruction and the killing of Sihon and Og's peoples?
hard.a:
These are among the hardest passages in the Old Testament, and they belong to a larger debate about the conquest. Some readers take the accounts as straightforward descriptions of divine judgment on nations whose wickedness had become complete (compare Genesis 15:16), carried out at a unique point in history and never to be repeated as a general policy. Others note that ancient war reports, including the Mesha Stele, often used sweeping language of total destruction as a conventional way of describing victory, so that the texts may not intend a literal account of every person killed. Still others read these passages as reflecting the limits of Israel's moral understanding at the time, later corrected by the fuller revelation of God in Christ; this last view is contested by those who hold that it undermines the authority of Scripture.

What can be said on any reading is that the Bible does not present these wars as a model for later believers, that Israel's own disobedience is judged in the same chapter, and that the New Testament directs God's people to fight not against flesh and blood (Ephesians 6:12). Readers who find these texts troubling are in good company, and the question deserves patient study rather than a quick answer.

questions: The people were saved by looking at an image of what was killing them. What does that suggest about facing the reality of sin rather than looking away?
Israel later turned the bronze serpent into an idol. What good gifts from God are you tempted to trust in place of God himself?
Jesus compared himself to the serpent lifted up. What does it mean for you to look to him in trust, especially when you feel you are dying of something you brought on yourself?
